extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of moral/periodical essays (educated general public; essayists)
extracted.subtask_description: Composing short, periodical moral or satirical essays that blend anecdotes, classical allusion, quotations, and explicit morals to instruct and entertain a general educated readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use classical exempla and quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Support observations with quotations and references to classical authors (Homer, Ovid, Virgil, Longinus, Juvenal, etc.) to provide authority and illustration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper repeatedly invokes and quotes ancient authors (long quoted verses and epigraphs) to exemplify virtues or morals and to lend weight to modern observations; interpose Latin epigraphs at the head of papers and sprinkle poetic lines within the prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerate and illustrate virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Present a short list of moral qualities (e.g., 'Discretion', 'Virtue', 'Good-Nature', 'Evenness of Temper') as necessary qualifications for the subject under discussion (here, a good husband/wife).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the virtue as a criterion and then illustrate it with historical or literary exemplars (Homer's fidelity, Brutus and Porcia for virtue, Caesar for humanity, Socrates and Marcus Aurelius for composed temper). Use such exemplars to make abstract virtues concrete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate letters and reader anecdotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use submitted letters or imagined correspondents as framing devices and source material for topics and examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many pieces begin with or include 'Mr. Spectator' letters that supply incidents, complaints, or local customs; the editor then comments on them. This provides immediacy, variety of voices, and a means to introduce multiple short stories or moral points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ vivid anecdote and detailed narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell concrete, often picturesque stories (customs, personal misfortunes, strange events) with particular sensory or procedural detail to engage the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long, specific narratives — e.g., the Bacon Flitch ceremony with its procedural steps and oath, Penelope's nightly unravelling, the Spanish nun's revenge — give texture and dramatize moral claims. Use names, places, ritual details and sample dialogue/text to increase verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize with dialogue, speeches, and formal texts
rubrics_metrics.description: Reproduce speech, oaths, registers, or direct discourse verbatim to dramatize events and reveal character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Register of Whichenovre is quoted in full formulaic language (oaths, procedural speech), and characters' speech (e.g., Penelope's web story, neighbours' depositions) is used to reveal hypocrisy, folly, or virtue; such reproductions function as mini-scenes within the essay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclude with an explicit moral or lesson
rubrics_metrics.description: End the speculation or anecdotal sequence by stating the lesson plainly: 'The Moral of the present Speculation amounts to this...' or an equivalent summation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After presenting examples and stories, the author draws together the point in a brief, declarative moral sentence that makes the essay didactic as well as entertaining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparative historical and cultural examples to show universality
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrate a point by citing instances from diverse times and peoples (Greeks, Romans, Jews, modern English examples) to demonstrate that the truth is general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts Jewish, Grecian, Roman, and contemporary English notions to argue for universal moral truths (e.g., true greatness is seen by gods/spirits differently than by men). Employ cross-cultural reference to broaden appeal and authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ridicule social foibles with satire and irony
rubrics_metrics.description: Expose vanity, pretension, and family-pride through playful irony and mockery (e.g., 'Family Madness', pedigree satire).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use humorous exaggeration and ironic scenarios (pedigree parade, scarfs-as-foppery, bribed witnesses) to make social critique palatable and entertaining; balance censure with wit rather than angry invective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermix poetry and epigraphs for rhetorical flourish
rubrics_metrics.description: Preface or punctuate essays with short poetic extracts or epigraphs (often in Latin) to set tone or underscore the theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epigraphs function as thematic signposts and lend literary polish; occasional inserted verses within the essay heighten emotional effect and provide stylistic variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use shocking or sensational examples selectively for emotional impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Deploy startling anecdotes (murder, revenge, dramatic physical acts) to illustrate the extreme consequences of passions or moral failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Spanish nun story—spectral appearance, torn heart—serves as a cautionary tale; such tales should be vivid but used sparingly so they reinforce rather than overwhelms the essay's argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support claims with antiquarian or documentary detail for authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Cite registers, local customs, legal forms, and dated occurrences (e.g., 'The Register of Whichenovre-Hall', public mourning for Queen Anne) to ground the essay in verifiable tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long quotations of ceremonial language and procedural description (who swears, when the bacon is delivered, the precise oath) increase the credibility of the anecdote and provide texture; footnotes may clarify historical references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a consistent periodical structure and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow the serialized format (numbered paper, date, motto/epigraph, letter or anecdote, commentary, footnote) and maintain a composed, urbane voice that mixes instruction with entertainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The recurring formal elements (number and date headings, Latin mottos, reader letters, editorial reply, closing moral) establish reader expectation and allow different topics to be treated within a recognizable frame.
